title: Translation Heads: Disentangling meaning from language in LLM-based machine translation
claim: Comparing next-token distributions under clean versus corrupted prompts via teacher forcing and KL divergence reveals where the prompt change matters.
layout: Top-down flow, two parallel columns merging into shared LLM; KL arrows crossing at bottom
description: A top-down diagram with two parallel columns, one for the clean prompt and one for the corrupted prompt. At the top, each column shows a row of four blue token boxes reading 'Le chat est rouge'. Arrows lead down through a gray banner reading 'Use teacher-forcing to obtain the distribution of each i token, i < |Y|' into a central box labeled 'LLM', which shows three model-family logos. Below it, a second gray banner reads 'Distribution of each token i, i < |Y| conditioning on either prompt'. Arrows fan out into two rows of four tall boxes. The left boxes are green and the right boxes are red. Each box has horizontal bars of varying intensity, standing for per-token distributions. Bracketed arrows connect each green box to its red counterpart, labeled 'KL divergence' in large bold text at the bottom. The eye goes first to the colored boxes and the LLM logos.
caption: We consider two few-shot MT prompts: a clean prompt and a corrupted prompt (obtained in this case by mixing multiple target languages) and both ending with the same query. For each prompt, we apply teacher forcing and compute the token-level output distributions for the ground-truth query. At each target position, we measure the KL divergence between the distributions conditioned on the clean and corrupted prompts.
abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to explain how neural networks implement their capabilities, but the scale of Large Language Models (LLMs) has limited prior MI work in Machine Translation (MT) to word-level analyses. We study sentence-level MT from a mechanistic perspective by analyzing attention heads to understand how LLMs internally encode and distribute translation functions. We decompose MT into two subtasks: producing text in the target language (i.e. target language identification) and preserving the input sentence's meaning (i.e. sentence equivalence). Across three families of open-source models and 20 translation directions, we find that distinct, sparse sets of attention heads specialize in each subtask. Based on this insight, we construct subtask-specific steering vectors and show that modifying just 1% of the relevant heads enables instruction-free MT performance comparable to instruction-based prompting, while ablating these heads selectively disrupts their corresponding translation functions.
